zones.name: African Traditional
zones.subtitle: the orisha, the ancestors & the diviners
zones.blurb: The traditional religions of sub-Saharan Africa. The green here is a handful of pre-1931 bilingual transcriptions (Callaway, Bleek–Lloyd) that record diviners’ own words; the great divination corpora (Ifá, Fa) survive as oral verse and reach English only in modern copyright.

zones.name: The African Diaspora
zones.subtitle: the New World religions of the enslaved
zones.blurb: The faiths carried across the Atlantic. Rastafari is the anomaly — young enough to have written and published its own scriptures; the Afro-Caribbean and Brazilian religions are initiatory and oral, held rather than printed, with no public-domain text to map.

zones.name: Pacific & Oceanic
zones.subtitle: the atua, the mana & the creation chants
zones.blurb: The religions of Polynesia — the least ethically fraught pillar, because the tradition-bearers often held the pen themselves. Queen Liliʻuokalani translated the Kumulipo during her imprisonment; Māori and Hawaiian narrators shaped their own transcriptions.

Australian Aboriginal — the Dreaming (Tjukurpa)
chips.note: living, oral & secret-sacred; no fixed text — mapping would misrepresent & risk restricted material

zones.name: Native North America
zones.subtitle: living & often sacred-restricted
zones.blurb: The most delicate pillar. Public-domain ethnography exists, but several items are ceremonial texts the originating nations actively wish were not in circulation — copyright-free is not the same as ethically free. These are flagged, not celebrated.
